title: What is contract-first (spec-first) API development — write the OpenAPI spec as the single source of truth, generate the controller interfaces / client SDKs from it (e.g. `openapi-generator`), and diff the spec in CI to catch breaking changes before any code is written — and how does it differ from code-first (where the contract is implicit in the controllers and can change by accident)?
shortTitle: What is contract-first (spec-first) API development, and how does it differ from code-first

s1_definition.profdef: Contract-first, also called spec-first, API development means you author the API description, typically an OpenAPI document, as the single source of truth before writing any implementation. From that spec you generate server-side controller interfaces and client SDKs with a tool like `openapi-generator`, and you diff the spec in continuous integration to catch breaking changes before code is written. Code-first does the opposite: you write the controllers first and the contract is derived from, and implicit in, the code, which means the contract can change by accident whenever someone edits a controller.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India is building a new transfer service that many teams will call. In contract-first, the teams first agree on an exact written blueprint of the API, like an architect's drawing, and everyone builds their part from that same drawing, with a reviewer checking any change to the drawing for anything that would break existing buildings. In code-first, one team just starts pouring concrete, and the blueprint is whatever they happened to build, so when they move a wall nobody notices until the neighbouring building's door no longer lines up.
s1_definition.oneliner: Contract-first writes the spec first as the single source of truth, generates code and SDKs from it, and diffs it in CI to catch breaks early; code-first lets the contract emerge from the controllers where it can change by accident.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Contract-first, also called spec-first, API development means you author the API description, typically an OpenAPI document, as the single source of truth before writing any implementation. From that spec you generate server-side controller interfaces and client SDKs with a tool like `openapi-generator`, and you diff the spec in continuous integration to catch breaking changes before code is written. Code-first does the opposite: you write the controllers first and the contract is derived from, and implicit in, the code, which means the contract can change by accident whenever someone edits a controller.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India is building a new transfer service that many teams will call. In contract-first, the teams first agree on an exact written blueprint of the API, like an architect's drawing, and everyone builds their part from that same drawing, with a reviewer checking any change to the drawing for anything that would break existing buildings. In code-first, one team just starts pouring concrete, and the blueprint is whatever they happened to build, so when they move a wall nobody notices until the neighbouring building's door no longer lines up.

**One line to remember:** Contract-first writes the spec first as the single source of truth, generates code and SDKs from it, and diffs it in CI to catch breaks early; code-first lets the contract emerge from the controllers where it can change by accident.

sections.s2_technical:
In contract-first, the OpenAPI document is a real artifact that lives in version control and is reviewed like code. It declares every path, method, request body, response body, status codes, and data schemas. Because it exists before implementation, it becomes a negotiation point: the provider team and every consumer team can agree on the shape of the API up front, in parallel, instead of the consumers waiting for the server to be built. A front-end team can generate a client SDK and start coding against a mock server generated from the spec while the back-end team is still implementing, which compresses the timeline and removes the guesswork about what the API will look like.

Code generation is central. With a tool like `openapi-generator` or the OpenAPI Generator Maven or Gradle plugin, you generate server stubs, which are Java interfaces and model classes your controllers implement, and you generate typed client SDKs for consumers in many languages. Because both sides are generated from the same spec, drift between what the server offers and what the client expects is eliminated by construction. The developer's job becomes implementing the generated interface's methods, not hand-writing the request and response plumbing, and if the spec changes, regeneration immediately surfaces a compile error wherever the implementation no longer matches.

Diffing the spec in CI is the safety net. On every change you compare the new spec to the baseline using an OpenAPI diff tool, and the pipeline classifies changes as compatible or breaking. Adding an optional field or a new endpoint is compatible and passes; removing a field, making one required, or changing a type is breaking and fails the build, forcing an explicit decision rather than an accidental outage. This is the crucial advantage: breaking changes are caught before code is even written, when they are cheapest to reconsider.

Code-first is the common default where you annotate Spring controllers and a library like springdoc generates the OpenAPI document from the running code. It is fast to start and keeps the spec in sync with the code automatically, which is genuinely convenient for small internal services. The weakness is that the contract is a side effect of the implementation, so it has no independent authority. A developer renaming a field, changing a return type, or tightening a validation does so in code and the contract silently follows, and unless there is separate contract testing, consumers only discover the break at runtime. The contract can change by accident because nothing guards it as a first-class artifact.

Senior nuances: contract-first shines for public or cross-team APIs where many consumers depend on stability and parallel development matters, while code-first is reasonable for a single team's internal service that changes rapidly and has few external consumers. The two are not mutually exclusive; a pragmatic middle ground is code-first with the generated spec committed and diffed in CI, giving some of the guardrails without full spec authoring. Whatever you choose, the real goal is that breaking changes require a deliberate, reviewed decision rather than slipping through as an ordinary code edit.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India is building a new transfer API that the mobile team, the partner-integration team, and an internal fraud service will all consume. If the teams wait for the server before they know the shape, they all serialize and the project slows down. This is exactly what contract-first solves: the OpenAPI spec is agreed first, so every team generates its own code from it and builds in parallel.

Problem 2 — In a previous code-first service, a developer renamed a response field from `txnId` to `transferId` during a refactor, and the contract silently changed with the code, so the partner integration broke in production. This is exactly the accidental-break weakness of code-first that spec diffing in CI prevents.

Problem 3 — The team wants new fields to be allowed freely but any removal or type change to be blocked automatically. This is exactly the spec-diff gate: additive changes pass CI, breaking changes fail CI before merge.

Our mini-project demonstrates the contract-first idea in a runnable way without a live network. The code represents an OpenAPI spec as a structured object, a `SpecDiffer` that classifies a proposed change as compatible or breaking exactly as a CI gate would, a generated-style `TransferApi` interface that a controller implements, and a demo that shows an additive change passing and a breaking change being rejected before any implementation runs.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a baseline spec for `TransferResponse` with required fields `transferId` and `status`, plus two proposed changes, one additive and one breaking.

Step 1: The baseline spec is loaded as the agreed source of truth. Every team's generated code is derived from this exact description, so there is a single shared understanding of the API before anyone writes an implementation.

Step 2: The first proposed change adds an optional field `feeCharged`. The spec differ compares old and new: no existing field was removed and no new field was made required, so the change is classified compatible and the CI gate passes. Old consumers simply ignore the new field.

Step 3: The second proposed change renames `transferId` to `txnId`, which from the schema's point of view removes the required field `transferId`. The differ detects that an existing field is gone, classifies the change as breaking, and the CI gate fails the build. This happens before any implementation code is written, which is the entire point: the break is caught at its cheapest moment.

Step 4: Separately, the controller implements the generated `TransferApi` interface. Because the interface is generated from the spec, if the spec ever changes the method signature, the controller stops compiling, so server drift from the contract is caught at build time rather than in production.

Step 5: The demo shows the additive change accepted, the breaking change rejected with a clear message, and the controller satisfying the generated contract, which together demonstrate how contract-first makes breakage a deliberate, reviewed event instead of an accident.

```
2026-10-24 14:44:30 INFO    CI gate — additive change (feeCharged) compatible? true
2026-10-24 14:44:30 SEVERE  CI gate — BREAKING change rejected BEFORE code is written: 'transferId' removed. Bump version or keep the field.
2026-10-24 14:44:30 INFO    Controller implements generated TransferApi: {transferId=TXF-00001, status=COMPLETED}
```
sections.s5b_flow:

```

sections.s5d_lld:

  ═══ LLD — Contract-First vs Code-First (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Single Source of Truth: the OpenAPI spec                     │
  │   WHY: server + all clients generated from one artifact      │
  │ Generated Interface (Template): controller implements stub   │
  │   WHY: drift from contract becomes a compile error           │
  │ Policy Gate: SpecDiffer classifies compatible vs breaking    │
  │   WHY: breaking changes need a deliberate decision           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: SpecDiffer only classifies; Controller only implements     │
  │ O: new endpoint = new spec path + generated method            │
  │ L: any controller implementing TransferApi is substitutable   │
  │ D: controller depends on generated interface, not plumbing    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────────────┐   compares   ┌──────────────────┐
  │ SpecDiffer        │────────────▶│ ApiSpec           │
  │ + isCompatible()  │              │ fields, required  │
  └──────────────────┘              └──────────────────┘
  ┌──────────────────┐   implements  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ TransferController│────────────▶ │ <<interface>>     │
  │ + createTransfer()│              │ TransferApi (gen) │
  └──────────────────┘              └──────────────────┘

  ── Decision Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────
  Public/cross-team API, many consumers, parallel work? → contract-first
  Single team, fast-changing internal service?          → code-first (ok)
  Want code-first but safe?  → commit generated spec + diff in CI

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. isCompatible(baseline, additive)  → true  (feeCharged added)
  2. isCompatible(baseline, breaking)  → false (transferId removed)
  3. controller.createTransfer(...)     → satisfies generated interface
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Contract-first, or spec-first, means I author the API description, normally an OpenAPI document, as the single source of truth before I write any implementation. That spec lives in version control and is reviewed like code. From it I generate the server-side controller interfaces and model classes that my controllers implement, and I generate typed client SDKs for every consumer, using a tool like openapi-generator. Because both the server and the clients are generated from the same spec, drift between what the server offers and what a client expects is eliminated by construction, and if the spec changes, regeneration immediately produces a compile error wherever the implementation no longer matches.

The biggest practical wins are parallel development and early breakage detection. Because the contract is agreed up front, the mobile team, the partner team, and the back-end team can all build at the same time, with front-end developers coding against a generated mock server while the server is still being written, instead of everyone serializing on the implementation. And I diff the spec in continuous integration against the baseline, so the pipeline classifies each change as compatible or breaking: adding an optional field or a new endpoint passes, while removing a field, making one required, or changing a type fails the build. That means breaking changes are caught before any code is written, when they are cheapest to reconsider.

Code-first is the opposite and is the common default, where I annotate Spring controllers and a library like springdoc derives the OpenAPI document from the running code. It is fast to start and keeps the spec automatically in sync, which is genuinely convenient for a small internal service. The weakness is that the contract is a side effect of the implementation, so it has no independent authority: a developer renaming a field or changing a return type during a refactor changes the contract silently, and unless I have separate contract testing, consumers only find out at runtime. In other words the contract can change by accident because nothing guards it as a first-class artifact.

On my project at National Bank of India we had exactly that failure once in a code-first service, where a refactor renamed a response field and silently broke a partner integration in production. So for the new transfer API, which the mobile team, a partner team, and an internal fraud service all consume, we went contract-first: we agreed the OpenAPI spec first, every team generated its own code from it, and we added an openapi-diff gate in CI that passes additive changes and fails removals or type changes before merge. That turned breakage from an accidental code edit into a deliberate, reviewed decision.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that contract-first writes the spec first as the single source of truth, generates both server stubs and client SDKs from it, and diffs it in CI so breaking changes are caught before code exists, whereas code-first lets the contract emerge implicitly from the controllers where it can change by accident, so I choose contract-first for public or cross-team APIs and code-first only for fast-changing internal services.
